entities.summary:
Count Michał Jerzy Wandalin Mniszech (1748–1806) was a prominent Polish nobleman, military officer, and statesman who served as Grand Marshal of the Crown from 1783 until the final partition of Poland in 1795. Born into the influential Mniszech family, one of the wealthiest and most politically connected magnate families of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, his career spanned the tumultuous decades leading to the nation's demise. His tenure as Grand Marshal placed him at the heart of the royal court in Warsaw, where he wielded significant administrative and ceremonial authority, embodying the power of the high aristocracy during a period of escalating foreign interference and internal reform efforts.

Mniszech began his public life with a military commission, participating in the Seven Years' War, a conflict that deeply reshaped European power dynamics and exposed the vulnerabilities of the Commonwealth. Following his military service, he transitioned into civil administration and estate management, actively modernizing the agricultural practices on his vast family holdings, particularly in Volhynia, which enhanced the Mniszech family's already considerable economic standing. This pragmatic approach to land management distinguished him from many contemporaries, demonstrating a forward-thinking engagement with the Enlightenment-era emphasis on rational economic improvement.

His political influence extended beyond mere courtly duties; Mniszech was a steadfast supporter of King Stanisław August Poniatowski and played a role in the efforts to maintain Polish sovereignty amidst Russian, Prussian, and Austrian pressures. While he did not prevent the partitions, his administrative actions and diplomatic engagements reflect the desperate struggles of the Polish elite to adapt and survive. His patronage of the arts and sciences, typical of enlightened magnates, also contributed to Warsaw's cultural vibrancy in its twilight years as an independent capital.

entities.summary:
Count Michał Jerzy Wandalin Mniszech (1748–1806) was a prominent magnate and statesman of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, whose career spanned the tumultuous final decades leading to its complete dissolution. Born into the immensely wealthy Mniszech family at Vyshnivets, he inherited vast estates and significant political influence, positioning him as a key player in the intricate power struggles that defined 18th-century Central European politics. His trajectory from a trusted advisor to King Stanisław August Poniatowski to a controversial figure who aligned with the Targowica Confederation illuminates the deep internal divisions and external pressures that ultimately led to Poland's demise. Mniszech's life serves as a microcosm of the Polish nobility's struggle to adapt to Enlightenment ideals while grappling with the encroaching imperial ambitions of Russia, Prussia, and Austria.

Mniszech ascended through the Commonwealth's administrative ranks, becoming Grand Secretary of Lithuania in 1778 and Grand Marshal of the Crown in 1783, a powerful position responsible for the royal court and security. He initially supported King Stanisław August Poniatowski's reform efforts, including participation in the Permanent Council, an executive body designed to streamline governance. His personal wealth allowed him to be a lavish patron of the arts, accumulating a renowned library of over 15,000 volumes and sponsoring theatrical productions. However, his political loyalties shifted dramatically as the Commonwealth faced existential threats. He became a vocal opponent of the Constitution of 3 May 1791, viewing it as an infringement on noble liberties, and subsequently joined the pro-Russian Targowica Confederation in 1792, an act widely regarded as a betrayal that precipitated the Second Partition of Poland.
